title: Roman ‘doubt’ targets application and disposition, not God’s promised benevolence in general
source_text: XXIX. Itaque Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae non habent dubitationem, sive diffidentiam, de gratia Dei, & ejus erga nos benevolentia, prout in genere consideratur, & verbo Dei proponitur: sed de nostra erga Deum dispositione, & de applicatione ad nos particulariter ejus promissorum. Nec volunt fideles perpetuo fluctuare & haesitare, an sint in Dei gratia; sed volunt eos firmiter assentiri, se esse in gratia, modo seriose seipsos examinent, & in se inveniant signa verae fidei & poenitentiae: etsi interim fateantur aliquam formidinem oppositae partis cum ea persuasione consistere posse, quia de propria dispositione non sumus aeque certi ac de Dei promissis. Quod ipsum, ut jam dictum, etiam a multis Protestantiibus conceditur, qui distinguunt inter certitudinem fidei qua articuli creduntur, & certitudinem illam reflexam qua quis de propria justificatione persuadetur.
pass_a_gloss: And so the doctors of the Roman Church do not have doubt or distrust concerning the grace of God and his benevolence toward us, as it is considered in general and proposed in God’s word: but concerning our disposition toward God, and concerning the application to us particularly of his promises. Nor do they wish the faithful perpetually to fluctuate and hesitate whether they are in God’s grace; but they wish them firmly to assent that they are in grace, provided they seriously examine themselves and find in themselves the signs of true faith and repentance: although in the meantime they confess that some fear of the opposite side can consist with that persuasion, because we are not equally certain of our own disposition as of God’s promises. Which very thing, as already said, is also conceded by many Protestants, who distinguish between the certainty of faith by which articles are believed and that reflex certainty by which someone is persuaded of his own justification.
pass_b_english: Romans do not distrust God’s general promised mercy; their caution concerns personal disposition and application.
They want firm assent from examined signs of faith and repentance, admitting residual fear—much as many Protestants distinguish direct and reflex certainty.
